blocks.content: Meghalaya's culture chapter is anchored by its rich, name-dense festival calendar — each of the three principal communities has its own major festival — alongside distinctive megalithic (monolith) traditions found across the Khasi and Jaintia Hills.

cells: The 'Hundred Drums Festival' — Garo post-harvest thanksgiving festival honouring Saljong, the sun-god of fertility; features massed traditional drumming and dance, among the most visually iconic festivals of North-East India

Annual thanksgiving dance festival in Shillong, celebrating peace, prosperity and thanksgiving to God, featuring distinctive Khasi dance performed by unmarried young men and women in traditional attire
Major Jaintia Hills festival (centred at Jowai) to drive away evil spirits/disease and pray for a good harvest, featuring symbolic wooden structures and ritual activities

A religious harvest-thanksgiving dance festival performed at Smit, near Shillong, associated with the Hima Khyrim Syiemship (Chapter 2), involving both religious ritual and traditional dance performance

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Wangala ('Hundred Drums Festival', Garo), Shad Suk Mynsiem (Khasi), and Behdienkhlam (Jaintia, at Jowai) are the three flagship festivals, one per principal community — a reliable, frequently tested one-to-one pairing.

The Khasi and Jaintia Hills feature one of India's most extensive traditions of megalithic monument-building, with clusters of standing stones (monoliths) erected historically to commemorate ancestors, mark significant events, or serve ceremonial functions — the village of Nartiang (Jaintia Hills) is particularly renowned for hosting one of the largest concentrations of such monoliths in the region, some standing several metres tall. This living megalithic tradition (monolith-erection continuing into more recent times in some communities) is a distinctive cultural-archaeological feature setting Meghalaya apart within India.

items: Meghalaya, and Shillong in particular, has a strong contemporary Western/rock music culture and has been popularly nicknamed the 'Rock Capital of India', reflecting a historically strong local following for guitar-based rock and blues music, alongside traditional indigenous music forms.
Traditional bamboo and cane craft, Khasi textile weaving, and Garo traditional dress and ornamentation are significant craft traditions across the state's communities.

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Shillong is popularly nicknamed the 'Rock Capital of India' for its strong contemporary rock/Western-music culture — a frequently tested pop-culture/tourism fact for the state capital.
